hook.text: Here's the LLM design prompt in its usual form: an assistant that answers questions from a company's documents, and can file a support ticket. It's fast now, and cheap. Is it any good?

hook-hard.text: A classifier has one right label per example. This has many good answers to every question, and more bad ones, so measuring it is a design problem of its own. Six questions.

q1.text: Question one. How do you evaluate an LLM application? In layers, from cheap to expensive.

q1-set.text: First, an offline eval set: realistic inputs, each with a reference answer or a rubric. A hundred or two well-chosen cases beat thousands of synthetic ones, and the set grows from real production failures.

q1-score.text: Second, scoring matched to the task: exact match or execution for structured output like JSON, SQL or code, retrieval metrics for search, and a rubric-driven LLM judge for open-ended text.
q1-score.spoken: Second, scoring matched to the task: exact match or execution for structured output like jay-son, sequel or code, retrieval metrics for search, and a rubric-driven LLM judge for open-ended text.

q1-ours.text: For the assistant, whether a ticket was filed with the right fields can be checked exactly. Whether it explained a policy correctly needs the judge.

q1-human.text: Third, human review of a sample, to catch what the metrics miss and to check the judge.

q1-ci.text: Fourth, evals as CI: rerun the suite on every prompt, model or retrieval change, and block regressions.

q1-online.text: Fifth, online: A B tests on user outcomes, with guardrails on latency, cost and refusal rate.

q1-bench.text: And public benchmarks are a weak guide to your task: many are saturated, and their test items may have leaked into training data.

q2-in.text: Several of those layers lean on an LLM judge, so the judge comes next.

q2.text: Question two. When can you trust an LLM as a judge? Only after you've measured it.

q2-bias.text: Zheng and colleagues tested judges for three biases: position, favoring the answer shown first; verbosity, favoring the longer one; and self-enhancement, favoring its own answers. The first two showed up clearly; the third was inconclusive, but worth guarding against.

q2-case.text: Here's position bias in numbers. A judge prefers version A of the assistant, shown first, over version B in seventy percent of pairs. Rerun every pair with B shown first, and B wins sixty-five percent.

q2-read.text: The answers didn't change, only their order. Whichever goes first wins about two thirds of the time, and at least thirty-five percent of the verdicts flipped with the order.

q2-fix.text: So score each pair in both orders, and count a win only when the two verdicts agree. Grade against a specific pass-fail rubric, not a score from one to ten. And use a judge from a different model family than the system it grades.

q2-cal.text: Then calibrate it against people. Experts label a sample, and you report the judge's agreement with them, corrected for chance with Cohen's kappa, before you rely on its scores.

q2-again.text: Change the judge's model or its rubric, and it's a new instrument: calibrate it again.

q3-in.text: But a judge grades the answer, not whether the right passage was ever found.

q3.text: Question three. How do you evaluate a RAG system? Retrieval-augmented generation has two halves, so measure each one, and a failure points at its cause.

q3-retrieval.text: Retrieval comes first, over a labeled set of queries and their relevant documents. Recall at k: did the right documents make the top k? And MRR, the mean reciprocal rank: how high did the first relevant one rank?

q3-example.text: Take three queries, each with one right document. The right one ranks first, third, and nowhere. Recall at five is two in three. MRR averages one, a third and zero: point four four.

q3-generation.text: Then generation. Faithfulness: is every claim supported by the retrieved passages? Answer relevance: does it address the question? And citation accuracy.

q3-faith.text: Faithfulness is judged against the passages, not against the truth. So a right answer the passages don't support still fails, because it's one you can't check.

q3-follow.text: The follow-up: answers are wrong, and recall at five is point four five. Rewriting the prompt won't help, because more than half the time the right passage never reached the model. Fix retrieval first, with better chunking, hybrid keyword search, or a reranker.

q3-middle.text: And don't just pass the top fifty instead. Models use the start and end of a long context better than the middle, so a few well-ranked passages often beat many loosely relevant ones. That's why a reranker earns its latency.

q4-in.text: Filing the ticket is where the assistant stops answering and starts acting.

q4.text: Question four. What is an agent, and how does tool calling work? Tool calling lets a model request an action instead of answering: it emits a structured call, a tool name and JSON arguments, and the application runs it and puts the result back into the context.
q4.spoken: Question four. What is an agent, and how does tool calling work? Tool calling lets a model request an action instead of answering: it emits a structured call, a tool name and jay-son arguments, and the application runs it and puts the result back into the context.

q4-loop.text: An agent is that loop, repeated until the model decides it's done. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard for exposing tools and data to models, so one integration serves many clients.

q4-design.text: Interviewers listen for the design around the loop: a budget on steps and cost, timeouts and retries for each tool, permissions scoped to the user, and a trace of every step.

q4-idem.text: And idempotent tools, since a retried step can run twice.

q4-compound.text: Then reliability, which compounds. If each step succeeds ninety-five percent of the time, a ten-step task succeeds about sixty percent of the time.

q4-fewer.text: Make each step ninety-nine percent reliable, and ten steps reach ninety. Or cut the task to five steps, and it's seventy-seven. Fewer, more reliable steps beat a clever long chain.

q5-in.text: And an agent that acts is graded on what it did.

q5.text: Question five. How do you evaluate an agent? Check outcomes, not prose: did the ticket get filed, do the tests pass, is the database in the state you expected?

q5-code.text: Those are checked with code, not a judge: the ticket exists with the right fields, or it doesn't.

q5-traj.text: Then inspect the trajectory: the right tool, valid arguments, the number of steps, the cost. An outcome check alone would pass an agent that got there by a path you'd never allow.

q5-repeat.text: Runs aren't deterministic, so repeat each task. The authors of tau-bench separate two scores: pass at k, at least one of k attempts succeeds, and pass hat k, all k succeed.

q5-numbers.text: Say each attempt succeeds four times in five, independently. Pass at four is over ninety-nine percent. Pass hat four is forty-one.

q5-which.text: A customer meets every attempt, not the best one, so a customer-facing agent needs pass hat k. And it falls fast: at eight attempts, seventeen percent.

q6-in.text: Last, the call that comes before any of this.

q6.text: Question six. When should you not use an LLM? When a smaller model or a rule does the job better on the axes that matter.

q6-list.text: That means tabular prediction, a strict latency or cost budget, a need for calibrated probabilities or for explanations a regulator will accept, or a task a regular expression solves.

q6-middle.text: A common middle path: use an LLM to label data, then train a small, fast classifier on those labels. You pay for the LLM once per label, not once per request.

q6-check.text: But check the labels against a sample people labeled first. The labeler is a judge, so question two applies to it too.

q6-why.text: This is the question that separates candidates who have shipped from those who have only prototyped.

close.text: From bias and variance to agents, every round on this track asks two things: will it hold up on data it hasn't seen, and how would you know?

close-practice.text: To find the rounds that still need work, try each page's concept checks, and the hundred and ten multiple-choice questions that close the track.

q4-inject.text: And treat what a tool brings back as untrusted: a retrieved page can carry instructions the model may follow, so an agent that reads outside content shouldn't also hold tools that do damage without a confirmation.

q1-agree-fix.text: When a change wins offline and loses online, and the guardrails held, fix the eval set: it's measuring something users don't care about.

q2-bar.text: The bar: it should agree with the experts about as well as they agree with each other.

q4-idem-key.text: Give each call an idempotency key, so filing the same ticket twice still leaves one ticket.
